sections.title: Before reading: study the Chapter 2 packets in How to read. The book without a wrapper.

segments.text: 安失小書。寧見人。人持小書行，寧視小書。人止，還小書；寧取小書。寧有一書，人無書。
寧持小書入門。門開，人入門。安持大書，寧持小書；人持帙，立。安有書，無帙。人有帙，無書。

inference_aids.alt: The large book lacks a wrapper.
inference_aids.art_brief: Inside the open doorway, An holds the large book without wrapper; Ning carries the small wrapped book; visitor stands with a separate loose wrapper. No extra leaves, no readable text.

segments.text: 安視帙，寧開小書。小書有帙，大書無帙。寧持小書帙，安視二帙。人立，視大書。
人開帙，安坐，開大書。帙有字，書有字，帙無名。帙字少，書字多；帙字、書字異。安視帙字，止。
寧閉小書，視大書。大書有破葉，帙有半葉。人持帙，寧取半葉。安持大書，視半葉。

exercises.title: Possession and absence
exercises.instruction: New miniature incidents, not story questions. Complete each sentence in Chinese. Cues: 1: Ning has a wrapper (yǒu); 2: the person has no small book (wú); 3: An lacks a wrapper (wú); 4: An has written characters (yǒu); 5: An has a large book (yǒu).

obrazec.rule: A person has a wrapper. Choose the positive existence verb; the opposite would deny the cue.

exercises.title: What is carried or inspected?
exercises.instruction: New miniature incidents, not story questions. Complete each sentence in Chinese. Cues: 1: Ning inspects a damaged leaf (pò yè); 2: An holds half a leaf (bàn yè); 3: Ning takes a book wrapper (shū zhì); 4: An sees a name (míng); 5: An has a small book (xiǎo shū).

obrazec.rule: Use the named object, not the action: a book has written characters.

sections.title: Two pieces do not yet make a whole

segments.text: 寧開小書，安取全葉。寧持半葉，安持全葉。全葉有多字，半葉有少字。安還全葉，寧取全葉。

inference_aids.alt: Whole and partial leaves are compared.
inference_aids.art_brief: Ning has just opened the small book; An takes a whole leaf from it. Ning holds the torn half leaf taken from the visitor’s wrapper. The visitor retains the loose wrapper. Show comparison, without asserting that the pieces join or that anyone owns the book. No readable text.

segments.text: 全葉、半葉有異字。寧視全葉，安視半葉。寧還全葉，安取全葉。寧閉小書，持半葉。人視二葉。
安視破葉，寧視半葉。破葉有半字，半葉有半字。寧還半葉，安取半葉。安持二葉，寧開小書。
小書無破葉。寧視全葉，見同字。
寧：「同字。」
segments.speaker: char-ning

segments.text: 安視二葉；全葉、半葉有同字。安止，視人。
安還全葉，寧取全葉。寧還小書，安取小書。小書葉少，大書葉多。安視破葉，寧持全葉。人閉帙，視半葉。

exercises.title: Keep the same existence pattern
exercises.instruction: New miniature incidents, not story questions. Complete each sentence in Chinese. Cues: 1: the person has a whole leaf (yǒu); 2: the wrapper has no damaged leaf (wú); 3: An has the small book wrapper (yǒu); 4: Ning has no half leaf (wú); 5: the small book bears a name (yǒu).

obrazec.rule: In this new incident the book lacks characters. The cue selects absence, not possession.

exercises.title: Whole, half, many and few
exercises.instruction: New miniature incidents, not story questions. Complete each sentence in Chinese. Cues: 1: Ning has a whole leaf (quán); 2: the person sees a half leaf (bàn); 3: An has few written characters (shǎo); 4: Ning looks at many characters (duō); 5: the person takes a whole leaf (quán).

obrazec.rule: Put the quantity before the noun: a half leaf, not a whole leaf.

sections.title: A name is evidence, not an owner

segments.text: 人持帙出門，寧立，視人。
安：「半葉。」
segments.speaker: char-an

segments.text: 人止，開帙。帙無半葉，安有半葉。安還半葉，人取半葉。
人持半葉，寧持全葉。半葉有名，全葉有名。寧視名，安視半葉。半葉有「寧」字，全葉有「寧」字。

inference_aids.alt: A matching written name draws attention.
inference_aids.art_brief: At the open doorway, visitor holds the half leaf and wrapper; Ning holds the whole leaf; An watches. Show traces of writing without readable invented letters. Both leaves contain writing; do not identify an owner.

segments.text: 寧取半葉，視「寧」字。寧有半葉，人有帙。帙無名，半葉有名；寧視帙，持半葉。
寧還半葉，安取半葉。安視名，寧視帙字。名同，帙字、書字異。安還大書，寧取大書。人閉帙，寧視門。
寧還全葉，安得全葉。全葉、半葉異，名同。安持小書，寧持大書。安閉小書，寧閉大書。人持帙，立。寧有大書，安有二葉；大書無帙，帙無名。

exercises.title: A name and a wrapper are different evidence
exercises.instruction: New miniature incidents, not story questions. Complete each sentence in Chinese. Cues: 1: the person sees the same written character (tóng zì); 2: An has a different written character (yì zì); 3: Ning holds a wrapper (zhì); 4: the small book has no name (míng); 5: the person has a damaged leaf (pò yè).

obrazec.rule: A new incident: a wrapper bears a name. Complete the existence clause.

exercises.title: Retrieve actions in new incidents
exercises.instruction: New miniature incidents, not story questions. Complete each sentence in Chinese. Cues: 1: Ning gives back a book wrapper (huán); 2: An takes a damaged leaf (qǔ); 3: Ning obtains a whole leaf (dé); 4: Ning closes a book (bì); 5: An loses custody of a wrapper (shī).

obrazec.rule: The cue names the action: see (jiàn), rather than look deliberately (shì).

cover.alt: Two books and a loose wrapper.
cover.art_brief: Fictional undated premodern doorway. An holds the large book without its wrapper. Ning holds the small book with its wrapper. The unnamed visitor has a separate loose wrapper. Three people, exactly two books and two wrappers; do not show the later name clue or readable writing.

grammar.title: 有書，無帙
grammar.rule: 安有書，無帙。人有帙，無書。

tables.caption: Read across: named subject, presence or absence, thing
A book can be the subject of the same presence/absence contrast

grammar.note_en:
Study Chapter 2 in How to read before beginning the story. The new form cards give meanings and modern Mandarin citation readings; the four packets and their attempts are separate preparation. The popups supply the meaning selected for each occurrence. This chapter contains constructed narration, not a quotation from an ancient author.

有 yǒu states that something is present or possessed. 無 wú states that it is absent or not possessed. A possessor is the person or thing presented as having something: in 安有書, “An has a book,” 安 is the possessor and 書 names what he has. In 安有書，無帙, “An has a book but no wrapper,” the second short clause continues An. The story contrasts this with 人有帙，無書, “the person has a wrapper but no book.” No extra word meaning English “has” or “does” is required. The written forms 有 and 無 do not change for different people.

A book can be the subject of the same pattern: 小書有帙 means “the small book has a wrapper”; 大書無帙 means “the large book has no wrapper.” The wrapper is a protective covering or case, not a page or leaf. 書有字 means “the book has writing,” and 帙有字 means “there is writing on the wrapper.” Here the thing bearing the writing is named first. There is no newly taught location preposition hiding in this translation. 無 gives an absence: 帙無名 is “the wrapper bears no name.” It is not a general-purpose way to negate every action verb. Other negative patterns come later.

Having a book or a wrapper does not establish legal ownership. 人有帙 tells us what the visitor has, not whose property it is. Likewise, returning a thing changes custody. The narration does not make the visitor a thief, nor does it prove that his loose wrapper belongs to the large book. The contrast between different writing on wrapper and book is evidence to examine, not an answer supplied by the narrator.

Some short noun expressions identify what is being handled. 書帙 means “a book wrapper,” 書葉 “a book leaf,” and 帙字 “the writing on a wrapper.” The identifying noun comes before the main noun. In 小書帙, “the small book’s wrapper,” 小 describes the book, not a newly established size of the wrapper. These are the bounded book-material combinations in this chapter; a broader possessive construction is taught later. Do not add an English-style apostrophe or a modern Chinese particle.

全葉 quán yè means “a whole leaf”; 半葉 bàn yè means “half a leaf.” 破葉 pò yè is “a damaged leaf.” A leaf is a physical part of the book, not the character printed on it. 多字 duō zì is “many written characters”; 少字 shǎo zì is “few written characters.” 少 has the citation reading shǎo here, not the later reading associated with youth. A damaged leaf can preserve only part of a written character: 半字, “half a character.” These concrete expressions do not teach a general system of measurement or counting words.

帙字少，書字多 means “the wrapper has few characters; the book has many.” The short descriptive words 少 and 多 can tell us about their preceding subject without an English verb “is.” 全葉、半葉有異字 means “the whole leaf and the half leaf have different characters”; later 有同字 means they have a character in common. Different writing in one place and matching writing in another are compatible: neither statement says every character matches. 同 tóng selects “same” here; no coordinated-action meaning “together” is required. 異 yì selects “different.”

A name is something written using characters. 半葉有「寧」字 means “the half leaf bears the character 寧”; the quotation marks identify the written form. The final discovery is that both the half leaf and the whole leaf show that character. 寧 is already the fellow learner’s name. 名同, “the names are the same,” summarizes that limited match. It does not say that Ning owns either book, wrote the name, or knows who did. A familiar name is the next problem, not a solved identity.

Track objects separately. The small book returns at the doorway. The large book remains without a wrapper. The visitor’s wrapper contains the half leaf, which changes hands during comparison. The whole leaf is taken from the small book. At the end An holds the two loose leaves and the small book; Ning holds the large book; the visitor has the loose wrapper. The grammar tables use actual clauses from these comparisons; they are references, not blanks to memorize.

obrazec.rule: Read the cue before selecting 有 or 無. These new incidents need not reproduce story facts. Cues: 1: the person has a large book; 2: the small book has no writing; 3: the person has a book wrapper; 4: An has no whole leaf. The worked example asserts that the named person HAS the object (yǒu).

The possessor precedes 有/無; the thing possessed follows it. Retain the stated contrast. Cues: 1: An has a whole leaf; 2: the large book has no whole leaf; 3: the person has no name recorded in this incident; 4: the book wrapper has writing. The worked example asserts that the named person HAS the object (yǒu).

B.title: Pensa B — Retrieve the named thing; the bank has three extras

obrazec.rule: New incidents. Use the whole word or short phrase named by the cue. Bank entries stay unchanged. 1: book wrapper (zhì); 2: name (míng); 3: whole leaf (quán yè); 4: half leaf (bàn yè); 5: many characters (duō zì); 6: few characters (shǎo zì); 7: damaged leaf (pò yè); 8: same written character (tóng zì). The worked example asks for a written character (zì).

C.title: Pensa C — Recall the changing evidence in Chinese sentences
C.instruction: Continue each scene cue with a complete Chinese sentence about the named person or object. Use the story, then compare with the model. A name, yes/no, or restatement of the cue is insufficient.

model_answers: 寧取小書。寧持小書入門。
items.rubric: Retrieve Ning taking the returned small book and/or bringing it inside. Require a complete event sentence; no bare name.
Retrieve the missing wrapper on the large book or contrast the visitor holding a wrapper while An holds the book. Do not infer that the loose wrapper belongs to either book.
Retrieve where the half leaf is found and/or Ning removing it from the wrapper. A statement that the book is damaged alone is insufficient.
Retrieve An taking the whole leaf from the small book or its fuller writing in contrast with the half leaf. The cue alone is not an answer.

Retrieve An calling attention to the half leaf, after which the visitor stops and opens the wrapper, and/or the subsequent return of the half leaf. The complete model return-event sentence is acceptable; do not claim that returning the leaf caused the earlier stop. Do not invent an accusation or motive.
Require the shared Ning character/name on both leaves. Merely saying there are two leaves or they have writing does not retrieve the distinguishing clue; do not infer ownership.

notes: Original constructed narration; no adapted or authentic quotation. No audio or generated image.
The existing Chapter 1 preparation remains intact; Chapter 2 adds four packets through the approved intro_en delivery. English and preparation do not earn narrative credit.
All twenty-four chapter1 recall IDs are used semantically in the new situation; the short opening loss clause connects the previous hook to its on-page recovery. No owner or motive is invented.
English grammar is intentionally substantial: it distinguishes possession, existence, noun grouping, partial writing and an evidentiary match.
Visible English meaning/readings cues select closed answers in new miniature incidents; full Pensa and workbook retained.
